docs.title: STCM — Synoptic Transform Calibration Model
docs.text: Welcome to the documentation for the Synoptic Transform Calibration Model, a computational research framework for investigating the Synoptic Problem through NLP embedding analysis.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text: STCM uses transformer-based embeddings of Ancient Greek text to test whether the double-tradition material (passages found in Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark) exhibits an embedding-space signature consistent with derivation from a shared written source — the hypothetical Q document (from German Quelle, "source").

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[SBLGNT Greek Text] --> B[Koine-Greek-BERT Embeddings]
    B --> C[Triple-Tradition Calibration]
    C --> D[Signature A: Independent baseline]
    C --> E[Signature B: Residual dependence]
    D --> F[Double-Tradition Scoring: centred cosine]
    E --> F
    F --> H[Permutation nulls: random, thematic, length-matched]
    F --> G[Covariates & directionality controls]
    G --> I[Results & Reports]
    H --> I

docs.title: Does STCM prove that Q existed?
docs.text: No. Computational linguistics cannot "prove" the historical existence of a lost document. What STCM demonstrates is that the geometry of the texts in high-dimensional semantic space is highly consistent with the mathematical signature of a shared written source, and strongly inconsistent with random or thematically matched pairing under our null models — even when tested against a thematically matched null model that controls for topical similarity. The results are consistent with some form of non-independent literary relationship (shared source and/or direct dependence). It provides strong statistical evidence in favour of the Q hypothesis, but it remains a model that tests consistency, not truth.

docs.title: Why use Koine-Greek-BERT?
docs.text: BERT models represent context-aware semantics, not just exact word overlap. Traditional stylometry often counts word frequencies, which fails to capture synonyms, morphological variations, or semantic themes. Koine-Greek-BERT has been pre-trained to understand the structure of Ancient Greek, allowing STCM to recognise when Matthew and Luke are saying the same thing in slightly different ways. An internal validation on known NT paraphrases confirms that the model produces sensible similarity judgements for the specific register and vocabulary of synoptic Greek.

docs.title: Doesn't the statistic just measure word overlap?
docs.text: No. The Pearson correlation between the centred cosines and traditional word-level Jaccard coefficients is substantial (r = 0.797) but meaningfully below 1.0. Approximately 37% of the variance is not explained by word overlap, indicating that the embedding analysis captures compositional, syntactic, and semantic structure that word counting cannot access.

docs.title: What about the circularity problem — aren't similar topics naturally similar?
docs.text: This was addressed with the thematic-null permutation test. Instead of pairing Matt–Luke pericopes randomly, this test pairs each Matthean pericope with a thematically similar Lukan pericope (wisdom with wisdom, apocalyptic with apocalyptic, etc.). The correctly paired pericopes still significantly exceed this thematic baseline (empirical p < 0.001, 1,000 permutations), demonstrating that the signal reflects genuine textual correspondence beyond mere topical similarity. A second kind of circularity is length: true parallels are of similar length, random pairs are not, and unrelated passages of different lengths are less similar than unrelated passages of equal length. Two further nulls therefore pair each Matthean pericope with a Lukan one of comparable length (optionally also of the same theme); the signal survives both (p < 0.001).

docs.title: Are the results sensitive to tuning?
docs.text: There is nothing to tune. The mean-centred cosine has no weights or free parameters, and it carries both the significance testing and the ranking. What could have been an arbitrary choice is the centring vector itself, so the two-tradition comparison is repeated under six definitions of it — all 240 vectors, double-tradition only, triple-tradition only, Mark only, a balanced mean of the two traditions, and Matthew and Luke only. The ordering is invariant across all six. An earlier version of this project used a weighted composite index; it has been retired from all inference and ranking and survives only as a legacy output.

docs.title: What if I don't have internet access to download the model?
docs.text: STCM includes an offline fallback, but it must be enabled explicitly. If ABeZet/Koine-Greek-BERT cannot be loaded via the transformers library, the pipeline stops with an error unless STCM_ALLOW_FALLBACK=1 is set, in which case a deterministic character-trigram hashing embedder (256-dimensional) is used. The fallback is sufficient to demonstrate that the pipeline runs end-to-end, but its results are not comparable to the published outputs; the embedder actually used is recorded in system_validation.txt.

docs.title: What is the Farrer Hypothesis and does STCM disprove it?
docs.text: The Farrer Hypothesis argues that Luke used Matthew as a source, meaning there is no "Q". STCM does not directly falsify this model. However, a Goulder redaction test compares pericopes that Goulder (1989) identifies as demonstrating Lukan redaction of Matthew against the rest. These pericopes show no statistically significant difference in centred-cosine distribution (Welch's t = −1.498, p = 0.164), but the test is underpowered (n = 10 vs. n = 41) and the medium-to-large effect size (Cohen's d = −0.767) indicates a potentially meaningful difference that the current sample cannot confirm or rule out. The result is therefore genuinely inconclusive — it neither supports nor refutes either hypothesis. A direct directionality test (which evangelist's embeddings predict the other's better, by leave-one-out ridge regression) was also built and controlled: it finds a small asymmetry in the double tradition, but the asymmetry depends on the ridge penalty, vanishes among pairs of equal length, and — decisively — the same statistic does not recover the known direction of copying where Matthew and Luke copy Mark. A method that fails its positive control is not allowed to answer the question, so STCM draws no directional inference.

docs.title: What about the possibility that Q was in Aramaic?
docs.text: Casey (2002) argues that Q may have been composed in Aramaic and translated independently into Greek. If so, the Greek-language embeddings would capture two independent translation events rather than the original source. This would attenuate the signal (making significant results more noteworthy, not less) and could explain why some pericopes score lower than expected despite being considered core Q material. It is also worth noting that a Koine Greek BERT model may be sensitive to the distinctive syntax of "translation Greek" — Semitisms and Aramaisms that arise when Greek renders Semitic source constructions. If Matthew and Luke translated an Aramaic Q independently, the resulting variance in Greek syntax would naturally lower cosine similarity, which is consistent with the spectrum of centred cosines observed across the double tradition.

docs.title: Does passage length or literary form drive the ranking?
docs.text: Length does not: the correlation between centred cosine and length in characters is essentially zero (r = 0.06), and the shortest and longest sayings occupy both ends of the ranking. Literary form does co-vary with the statistic (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.029): discourses agree most closely, parables least. This is reported as a covariate of the ranking; it may reflect the evangelists' freer handling of parables, or the model's handling of narrative-shaped sayings, and the corpus cannot separate the two. It is not a short-saying artefact, since the shortest form (the proverbial saying) is not the highest-scoring.

docs.title: How were the pericopes delimited?
docs.text: By the Aland synopsis and the IQP inventory, under three rules enforced by the loader: each pair is trimmed to the verses that are actually parallel (non-contiguous ranges such as Luke 3:7–9 + 16–17 are supported), no verse belongs to two units of the same set, and no verse of Matthew or Luke belongs to both the calibration and the test set. Mark–Q overlaps are excluded from the calibration set. The table has 51 double-tradition and 46 triple-tradition units; the article shows, with John's Preaching, how much a wrong boundary can move a single pericope.

docs.title: Can I run this on John or the non-canonical gospels?
docs.text: Yes, the pipeline can be adapted to any Greek text, but you will need to map the pericopes in data_loader.py (and add their metadata in stcm/metadata.py). Currently, it uses a hardcoded table based on the Aland Synopsis and the IQP inventory for the synoptic gospels.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11, 3.12, or 3.13
  • Git
  • uv (recommended) — or pip

docs.title: 1. Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/stcm-research/stcm.git
cd stcm

docs.title: 2. Create a virtual environment and install dependencies
docs.text:
With uv (recommended):

uv venv
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

Or with pip:

python -m venv .venv
# Windows:
.venv\Scripts\activate
# macOS/Linux:
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 3. Download the SBLGNT text
docs.text:
The SBL Greek New Testament text is required. It will be downloaded from the Logos Bible Software GitHub repository.

python download_sblgnt.py

This places matthew.txt, mark.txt, and luke.txt in data/raw/.

You are now ready to run the STCM pipeline.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: STCM operates as a computational pipeline applying modern NLP (Natural Language Processing) to Ancient Greek text.

docs.title: 0. Pericope Alignment
docs.text:
Pericopes are delimited by the Aland synopsis and, for the double tradition, the inventory of the International Q Project. Three rules are enforced by the loader (stcm/data_loader.py):

  • each Matthew–Luke pair is trimmed to the verses that are actually parallel; where one evangelist scatters the material the unit is assembled from non-contiguous ranges (Luke 3:7–9 + 16–17 against Matt 3:7–12; Matt 23:4, 6–7, 13, 23–36 against Luke 11:39–52);
  • no verse belongs to two units of the same set;
  • no verse of Matthew or Luke belongs to both the calibration and the test set — Q sayings embedded in Markan contexts are cut out of the calibration units, and Mark–Q overlaps (Temptation, Beelzebul, Mission charge) are excluded from calibration altogether.

The result is 46 triple-tradition and 51 double-tradition units. The SBLGNT critical-apparatus sigla (⸀ ⸂ ⸃ …), which are editorial marks rather than text, are stripped before encoding.

docs.title: 1. Text Representation (Embeddings)
docs.text:
We use ABeZet/Koine-Greek-BERT, a transformer model pre-trained on the Hellenistic and biblical Greek register to support semantic matching in ancient literature. Each pericope is encoded as one sequence, so every token is contextualised by the whole passage, with dropout disabled (evaluation mode). We extract the attention-masked mean of the last hidden state, giving a 768-dimensional vector normalised to unit length. Texts longer than the 512-token window (one double-tradition and nine calibration texts) are split at sentence boundaries into the fewest chunks that fit, each chunk is encoded in full, and the chunk vectors are averaged with token-count weights; nothing is truncated. Embeddings are cached under a key that includes the model, the encoding-scheme version and the normalised text.

If the transformer model cannot be loaded, the pipeline stops with an error; a deterministic 256-dimensional character-trigram hashing embedder can be enabled explicitly (STCM_ALLOW_FALLBACK=1) for smoke-testing only.

An internal validation on known triple-tradition parallels (Feeding of the Five Thousand across Matt/Mark, the Paralytic across Matt/Luke, the Transfiguration and the Baptism across Mark/Luke) against unrelated pairs confirms that the model discriminates known synoptic parallels from unrelated passages in the specific register of New Testament Greek (raw 0.964 vs 0.850; centred 0.48–0.76 vs 0.02–0.04). No double-tradition passage is used for validation, since that is the test set.

docs.title: 2. Calibration (Triple Tradition)
docs.text:
We analyse the 46 passages where Matthew, Mark, and Luke overlap with a plain Markan parallel. Assuming Markan priority, Matthew and Luke are independent derivations from Mark. We compute:

  • Signature A: The mean cosine similarity between Matthew and Luke (raw μ = 0.9571, σ = 0.0231, 95% CI [0.9500, 0.9637]; centred μ = 0.5681), giving us an expected baseline of similarity for texts drawn from the same source.
  • Signature B: The correlation of Matthew's residual (Matthew minus Mark) and Luke's residual (Luke minus Mark). This captures whether two authors make structurally similar modifications to a shared source (μ = 0.3542, σ = 0.1359).

For double-tradition pericopes (where Mark is absent), the residual is computed relative to the Mark centroid — the mean embedding of all Mark's triple-tradition pericopes. Mark's material is overwhelmingly narrative, whereas the double tradition is predominantly discourse, so any two sayings passages show correlated displacement against this narrative baseline. That elevation is measured directly as the genre floor — the mean residual correlation among mismatched double-tradition pairs (0.198) — and the evidential quantity is the matched-pair excess over it (0.756 − 0.198 = 0.558). The residual norm is not used as evidence: it is a near-deterministic function of passage length (Spearman ρ = −0.82).

docs.title: 3. Primary Statistic — Mean-Centred Cosine
docs.text:
Contextual embedding spaces are anisotropic: vectors crowd into a narrow cone, so even unrelated texts show high raw cosine similarity (Ethayarajh 2019). The primary statistic therefore subtracts the corpus mean vector, computed over all 240 pericope embeddings, before taking cosines (cf. Su et al. 2021):

centred cosine = cos(emb(Matt) − μ, emb(Luke) − μ)

This single, weight-free statistic carries all inference and ranking. Under it, unrelated pairs average 0.0517 while matched double-tradition pairs average 0.7171. The raw cosine is reported in parallel throughout and the residual correlation is analysed separately.

A legacy composite index (0.8 × cosine + 0.2 × max(0, residual)) survives only behind run_pipeline.py --legacy. It is not used for inference or ranking.

docs.title: 4. Comparing the Two Traditions
docs.text:
The corpus mean is not neutral between the traditions: 138 of the 240 vectors are triple-tradition, so the origin of the centred space lies nearer that material and centring shortens those vectors more (mean centred norm 0.3078 against 0.4045). Setting the two matched means side by side would therefore flatter the double tradition. Each set is instead measured against its own mismatched-pair floor.

On that basis the result does not depend on the anisotropy correction at all. In the raw space the matched means are nearly identical (0.9509 and 0.9571), but the triple-tradition floor is far higher (0.9064 against 0.8378), because that material is internally homogeneous narrative inherited from Mark. The excess over floor is 0.1131 against 0.0506; after centring, 0.6654 against 0.5165.

Two controls close the remaining gaps:

  • Nearest-neighbour floor — each pericope measured against the most similar passage it is not parallel to, which removes any advantage the double tradition might gain from being internally more varied. Because this is an order statistic and rises with pool size, the larger set (the double tradition, 51) is subsampled to the smaller (46) over 1,000 draws. Excess: 0.0473 against 0.0116 raw, 0.3371 against 0.1803 centred; none of the 1,000 draws falls to the triple-tradition value.
  • Centring sensitivity — the comparison is repeated under six definitions of the centring vector, including one that balances the traditions by construction. The ordering is invariant across all six.

docs.title: 5. Evaluation Suite
docs.text:
All tests below are computed on the mean-centred cosine, with the raw cosine reported in parallel (advanced_analysis.py):

  1. Random permutation test — 1,000 random Matt–Luke pairings produce a null distribution; the observed mean is tested against it (0.7171 vs null 0.0635, z = 27.3, empirical p < 0.001).
  2. Thematic-null permutation test — A more demanding null pairing each Matthean pericope with a thematically similar Lukan one (wisdom with wisdom, apocalyptic with apocalyptic), controlling for topical overlap. The signal survives (null 0.1098, z = 31.6, p < 0.001).
  3. Length-matched nulls — Correctly paired pericopes are of similar length (mean |log ratio| 0.22) whereas random pairs are not (0.85), and unrelated passages of unequal length are less similar than unrelated passages of equal length (ρ = −0.20 over the 2,550 mismatched pairs). Two nulls therefore pair each Matthean pericope with a Lukan one of comparable length (|log ratio| ≤ 0.4), from the whole set or from the same theme. The signal survives both (nulls 0.0924 and 0.1387; z = 28.3 and 29.2).
  4. Raw-cosine permutation tests — The same four nulls on the uncorrected cosine; fully concordant (0.9509 vs nulls 0.8398–0.8542, all p < 0.001).
  5. Residual-correlation permutation tests — The same four nulls on the residual correlation alone (0.7558 vs nulls 0.208–0.267, all p < 0.001).
  6. Cross-tradition floor comparison — Mismatched-pair floor for the triple tradition as well as the double, so each set is read against its own baseline.
  7. Nearest-neighbour floor with size matching — Controls for internal homogeneity; the larger set is subsampled to the smaller over 1,000 draws.
  8. Centring-vector sensitivity — Recomputes both traditions under six centring schemes.
  9. Sentence-level bootstrap — Resamples sentences within each pericope (200 resamples); mean perturbation SD 0.1227 on the centred scale.
  10. Covariates — Length in characters (r = 0.06, n.s.), form-critical class (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.029; discourse > narrative > proverbial > parable), Kloppenborg stratum (Q¹ vs Q² p = 0.956), word-level Jaccard overlap (r = 0.797; ~37% of variance unexplained).
  11. Goulder redaction test — Compares centred-cosine distributions for the pericopes Goulder (1989) identifies as showing Lukan redaction of Matthew against the remainder (Welch's t = −1.498, p = 0.164, Cohen's d = −0.767). Underpowered at n = 10 vs n = 41; genuinely inconclusive.
  12. Directionality inference — Leave-one-out ridge regression with intercept (hat-matrix identity), ridge penalty chosen by LOO error and reported across a grid, jackknife SE, sign-flip permutation test, plus two controls: a length-balanced subset and the known-direction case of the triple tradition (Mark → Matthew / Luke). The double-tradition asymmetry (ΔR² = +0.024, sign-flip p = 0.004) is regulariser-dependent, vanishes in length-balanced pairs (p = 0.58), and the statistic does not recover the known Markan direction (p = 0.73 / 0.68), so no directional inference is drawn.
  13. Internal BERT validation (legacy suite) — Model calibration on known triple-tradition parallels vs unrelated passage pairs (separation 0.114 in the uncorrected space).

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The outputs from STCM provide a calibrated, quantitative measurement of the literary relationship among the double-tradition texts: their geometry is consistent with derivation from a common written source, whilst not by itself adjudicating between the Two-Source and Farrer hypotheses. All figures on this page are from the version-2 run (October 2026: corrected alignment tables, chunked encoding, sigla stripped; 51 double-tradition and 46 triple-tradition pericopes). Earlier figures based on 36/49 pericopes are superseded.

docs.title: 1. Triple Tradition Baseline (Signature A)
docs.text: When analysing the 46 Triple Tradition pericopes where Matthew, Mark, and Luke all overlap with a plain Markan parallel, the mean cosine similarity between Matthew and Luke is 0.9571 (σ = 0.0231, 95% CI [0.9500, 0.9637]); after mean-centring the corpus (anisotropy correction) the baseline is 0.5681 (95% CI [0.5207, 0.6148]). Because we know under Markan priority that both authors drew from Mark, this gives us a quantitative measure of what a "shared source derivation" looks like in the Koine-Greek-BERT space. The residual correlation against each pericope's own Markan text (Signature B) averages 0.3542 (σ = 0.1359).

docs.title: 2. Double Tradition Scoring
docs.text:
The primary statistic for both inference and ranking is the mean-centred cosine similarity (anisotropy-corrected; no tunable parameters). Across the 51 Double Tradition pericopes the matched-pair mean is 0.7171 (SD 0.1737, range [0.1464, 0.9788]) against an unrelated-pair floor of 0.0517; the mean raw Matt–Luke cosine is 0.9509.

Top 5 pericopes by centred cosine:

  1. Serving Two Masters (0.9788)
  2. Harvest Plentiful (0.9549)
  3. Lament over Jerusalem (0.9441)
  4. Hidden from Wise, Revealed (0.9153)
  5. Return of Unclean Spirit (0.9086)

Full data for all 51 pericopes — with verse references, stratum, form, lengths and word overlap — is in outputs/reports/centred_cosine_ranking.csv and in the article (Appendix A, Table A1).

docs.title: 2b. Comparing the Two Traditions
docs.text:
The corpus mean used for centring is dominated by triple-tradition vectors (138 of 240), which shortens those vectors more (mean centred norm 0.3078 against 0.4045). Comparing the two matched means directly would therefore flatter the double tradition, so each set is measured against its own mismatched-pair floor.

Quantity Raw cosine Mean-centred Triple tradition: matched 0.9571 0.5681 Triple tradition: mismatched-pair floor 0.9064 0.0516 Triple tradition: nearest non-parallel floor 0.9455 0.3879 Triple tradition: excess over mean floor 0.0506 0.5165 Double tradition: matched 0.9509 0.7171 Double tradition: mismatched-pair floor 0.8378 0.0517 Double tradition: nearest non-parallel floor 0.9042 0.3846 Double tradition: excess over mean floor 0.1131 0.6654

The result does not depend on the anisotropy correction. In the raw space the two matched means are nearly identical, and what separates the traditions is the floor: the triple-tradition material is internally homogeneous narrative inherited from Mark, so any two of its passages already resemble one another closely.

Two controls close the obvious objections. Measuring each pericope against the most similar passage it is not parallel to removes any advantage the double tradition gains from being internally more varied; since that statistic rises with pool size, the larger set (the double tradition, 51) is subsampled to the smaller (46) over 1,000 draws. The excess is then 0.0473 [0.0439, 0.0506] against 0.0116 raw and 0.3371 [0.3168, 0.3589] against 0.1803 centred, and none of the 1,000 draws falls to the triple-tradition value. Repeating everything under six centring schemes leaves the ordering unchanged.

docs.title: Centred-Cosine Permutation Tests (Primary)
docs.text: Contextual embedding spaces are anisotropic — even unrelated passages average 0.838 raw cosine. After mean-centring, the unrelated-pair floor collapses to 0.052 while the matched-pair mean remains 0.717, widening the contrast from 0.113 to 0.665. Against 1,000 random permutations the observed mean (0.7171) far exceeds the null (0.0635, σ = 0.0239, z = 27.3, p < 0.001); against the thematic null — pairing each Matthean pericope with a thematically similar Lukan one — it likewise dominates (null 0.1098, σ = 0.0192, z = 31.6); and against the two length-matched nulls, which pair each Matthean pericope with a Lukan one of comparable length (true parallels are of similar length; random pairs are not), the result is the same (null 0.0924, z = 28.3; length-and-theme-matched null 0.1387, z = 29.2; all p < 0.001).

docs.title: Raw-Cosine Tests (Concordant)
docs.text: The same tests on the uncorrected cosine agree: observed 0.9509 vs random null 0.8398 (σ = 0.0041, z = 27.1), thematic null 0.8470 (z = 19.9), length-matched null 0.8466 (z = 22.8) and length-and-theme null 0.8542 (z = 27.0), all p < 0.001. The signal is neither an artefact of representation geometry, nor of topical similarity, nor of matched length.

docs.title: Residual Genre Floor
docs.text: The shared discourse-vs-narrative displacement against the Mark centroid is quantified directly: mismatched pairs average 0.198 residual correlation (the genre floor), matched pairs 0.756 — a pairing-specific excess of 0.558 (p < 0.001 against all four nulls). See outputs/reports/advanced_analysis.md.

docs.title: Sentence-Level Bootstrap
docs.text: Resampling sentences within each pericope (200 resamples) yields a mean perturbation standard deviation of 0.1227 on the centred-cosine scale — less than a fifth of the matched-minus-floor contrast (0.665). The broad shape of the distribution and the identity of the extremes are stable; fine rank distinctions between adjacent pericopes are not.

docs.title: Length, Form and Stratum
docs.text: Passage length (in characters of Greek text) is uncorrelated with the statistic (Pearson r = 0.060, p = 0.675; Spearman ρ = 0.091). Literary form is associated with it (Kruskal–Wallis H = 9.0, p = 0.029): discourses average 0.805 (n = 15), narratives 0.750 (4), proverbial sayings 0.688 (25), parables 0.573 (6). This is reported as a covariate of the ranking — parables are the form the evangelists rework most freely, but a representational explanation cannot be excluded — and it is not a short-saying artefact, since the shortest form is not the highest-scoring. Kloppenborg's strata are indistinguishable (Q¹ 0.717, n = 20; Q² 0.722, n = 26; Mann–Whitney p = 0.956).

docs.title: Word-Overlap Comparison
docs.text: The Pearson correlation between centred cosines and word-level Jaccard coefficients is substantial (r = 0.797) but meaningfully below 1.0 (~37% of variance unexplained), demonstrating that the embedding analysis captures semantic and syntactic structure beyond what traditional verbal-agreement statistics measure.

docs.title: Directionality
docs.text: Predicting Luke's embeddings from Matthew's (leave-one-out ridge with intercept, penalty α = 1 chosen by LOO error; R² = 0.233) works slightly better than the reverse (0.209): ΔR² = +0.024, jackknife 95% CI [−0.003, +0.050], sign-flip permutation p = 0.004. That asymmetry is not read as evidence of direction, for three reasons established by the controls: it shrinks monotonically with the ridge penalty (to zero at α ≥ 30); it disappears among the 30 pairs whose members are of comparable length (ΔR² = +0.010, p = 0.58) — the longer member of a pair is simply the better predictor; and the identical statistic fails to recover the known direction of copying in the triple tradition (Mark → Matthew ΔR² = +0.004, p = 0.73; Mark → Luke −0.005, p = 0.68). The residual-norm comparison used in an earlier version is likewise set aside: the residual norm is a near-deterministic function of passage length (Spearman ρ = −0.82).

docs.title: 5. Goulder Redaction Test
docs.text: The ten pericopes Goulder (1989) identifies as exhibiting Lukan redaction of Matthew show a lower mean centred cosine (0.6138) than the remaining 41 pericopes (0.7423), but the difference is not statistically significant (Welch's t = −1.498, p = 0.164, Cohen's d = −0.767). With group sizes of n = 10 vs. n = 41 the test is underpowered, and the result is genuinely inconclusive — it neither supports nor refutes the Farrer Hypothesis.

docs.title: 6. BERT Validation
docs.text: Four known triple-tradition parallels (no double-tradition passage is used, since that is the test set) produce high raw cosine similarities (mean 0.964); two unrelated passage pairs produce lower similarities (mean 0.850). The separation (0.114 in the uncorrected space) widens after mean-centring (parallels 0.48–0.76, unrelated pairs 0.02–0.04), confirming that the model is adequately calibrated for NT Greek.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The geometry of the Double Tradition in semantic space is highly non-random. Its relationship patterns closely mimic, and measured against each set's own floor exceed, the mathematical signatures of the known shared-source relationship observed in the Triple Tradition. The signal survives random, thematic and length-matched null tests on a single weight-free statistic, exceeds the quantified genre floor, and captures information beyond simple lexical overlap. Literary form co-varies with the ranking and is reported as such. The Goulder redaction test is inconclusive at this sample size, and the directionality statistic, having failed its positive control, is not used to infer who copied whom. Whilst this does not definitively prove a written document called Q, the embedding evidence is strongly inconsistent with random, thematically matched or length-matched pairing under our null models, and consistent with some form of non-independent literary relationship (shared source and/or direct dependence).

docs.title: The Synoptic Problem
docs.text: The Synoptic Problem is the challenge of explaining the extensive literary similarities and differences among the first three canonical gospels: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. They share common wording, order of events, and even parenthetical editorial comments, which strongly implies a literary relationship rather than merely independent reliance on oral tradition.

docs.title: The Two-Source Hypothesis (2SH)
docs.text:
The most widely accepted solution in modern scholarship is the Two-Source Hypothesis, which posits:

  1. Markan Priority: The Gospel of Mark was written first. Matthew and Luke independently used Mark as a primary narrative framework.
  2. The Q Source: Matthew and Luke also share about 235 verses of sayings material (the "Double Tradition") not found in Mark (e.g., the Lord's Prayer, the Beatitudes). The 2SH posits they independently drew this material from a lost written document of Jesus's sayings, designated Q (from the German Quelle, meaning "source").

docs.title: Farrer Hypothesis & Other Alternatives
docs.text: A significant minority of scholars reject Q, most notably through the Farrer Hypothesis. This model accepts Markan priority but argues that Luke used Matthew as a source (or vice versa), explaining the double tradition without postulating a lost document.

docs.title: How STCM Approaches the Problem
docs.text:
STCM does not attempt to "prove" Q. Instead, it tests whether the statistical distribution of the texts in high-dimensional embedding space is consistent with the Q hypothesis.

If Matthew and Luke both used Mark, we can observe exactly what a "shared source" relationship looks like mathematically by analysing the Triple Tradition. We use this to calibrate two signatures: - Signature A: The expected similarity between two texts drawn from a common written source. - Signature B: The expected correlation in how two different authors modify their common source.

We then measure the Double Tradition in the same space. The comparison that matters is not the raw level of similarity but the excess over each set's own floor: how much more alike true parallels are than unrelated passages of the same kind already are. On that measure the double tradition exceeds the Markan calibration set, in both the corrected and the uncorrected geometry. This is consistent with derivation from a shared written source; it does not by itself decide between Q and Luke's direct use of Matthew.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The entire STCM process is driven by run_pipeline.py. It is designed to be resumable and modular.

docs.title: Standard Run
docs.text:
To execute the entire pipeline from start to finish:

python run_pipeline.py

This will: 1. Load the SBLGNT texts and check the alignment tables (no verse in two units; no verse in both sets) 2. Load the embedding model lazily (only on a cache miss) 3. Calibrate on the Triple Tradition (46 pericopes) 4. Run the advanced analysis on the Double Tradition (51 pericopes): centred-cosine statistics, four permutation nulls, floors, covariates, directionality with controls 5. Draw Figures 1–6 6. Save all output to outputs/

docs.title: Legacy steps
docs.text:
The retired composite Q-score, the latent-Q reconstruction and the old evaluation suite are not part of the article. They run only on request:

python run_pipeline.py --legacy

docs.title: Resuming from Cache
docs.text:
If a previous run was interrupted or you only want to re-run the final evaluation steps, use the --resume flag. It reads logs/STEP_LOG.md to determine the last completed step and picks up from there.

python run_pipeline.py --resume

docs.title: Overriding Configuration
docs.text:
STCM uses environment variables for configuration. You can change the behavior without editing code:

Change the embedding model:

# Linux / macOS
STCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL=bert-base-multilingual-cased python run_pipeline.py

# Windows PowerShell
$env:STCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL="bert-base-multilingual-cased"
python run_pipeline.py

Increase log verbosity:

STCM_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG python run_pipeline.py

docs.title: Understanding Outputs
docs.text: Look in the outputs/ directory for your results: - reports/advanced_analysis.md — Every statistic in the article: calibration table, anisotropy table, permutation nulls, genre floor, directionality with controls, covariates, bootstrap. - reports/centred_cosine_ranking.csv — The per-pericope ranking with verse references, stratum, form, lengths and word overlap. - reports/key_stats.json — The handful of numbers the figure script needs. - figures/evaluation/fig1–fig6 — The article figure set. - reports/evaluation_summary.md, reports/q_score_distribution.csv, reports/system_validation.txt — legacy outputs (--legacy only).
